title: India's ₹37,500 Crore Coal Gasification Push Stalls as Industry Demands Guaranteed Buyers
excerpt: Companies say the government's 20% capital subsidy is not enough — they want assured offtake agreements, freight support, and land near coal mines before committing billions to gasification plants.
body:
• India's ₹37,500 crore ($3.92 billion) coal gasification incentive scheme, approved by the Cabinet in May 2026, faces resistance from industry players who say a 20% capital subsidy alone is not enough to justify massive upfront investments.
  • Companies want guaranteed offtake agreements — clarity on buyers, volumes, and prices — before committing thousands of crores to gasification plants with long gestation periods.
  • The scheme targets gasification of 75 million tonnes of coal annually, aiming to reduce India's dependence on imported LNG, urea, ammonia, and methanol. Applications close September 7, 2026.
  • State-run NTPC plans to produce 5–10 million tonnes of synthetic gas per year, but execution challenges at the Talcher fertiliser project in Odisha underscore the risks.

India's ambitious plan to build a domestic coal-to-chemicals industry is running into a fundamental objection from the companies it needs on board: show us the buyers first.

The ₹37,500 crore ($3.92 billion) Scheme for Promotion of Surface Coal/Lignite Gasification, approved by the Union Cabinet on May 13, 2026, offers financial assistance of up to 20% of the cost of plant and machinery. But industry executives told the Economic Times that the capital subsidy does not fully address the demand and market risks attached to projects requiring substantial upfront investment and years-long gestation periods.

What the Industry Wants

Developers are seeking assured offtake commitments from the government — binding agreements that would provide clarity on who will purchase the output, how much they will buy, and at what prices. Without predictable demand, companies say, the investment case for gasification plants remains weak despite the scale of government incentives.

Beyond guaranteed buyers, the industry is pushing for freight support and land allocation near coal mines and ports, particularly for projects supplying fertiliser and steel plants. Transportation and logistics costs could further erode project economics if facilities are built far from consumers or export infrastructure, according to Outlook Business.

"A capital subsidy does not fully address the demand and market risks attached to projects that require substantial upfront investment and have long gestation periods."

— Industry executives, via Economic Times

The Scale of Ambition

The scheme targets gasification of approximately 75 million tonnes of coal and lignite, contributing to India's broader goal of gasifying 100 million tonnes of coal by 2030. Coal gasification converts coal into synthetic gas (syngas), which can then be processed into cleaner fuels, chemicals, fertilisers, and hydrogen.

The government expects the programme to support around 25 projects, generate roughly 50,000 direct and indirect jobs in coal-producing regions, and yield approximately ₹6,300 crore in annual government revenue. Total investments catalysed are estimated at ₹2.5–3 lakh crore, according to the Ministry of Coal.

India imports more than 83% of its crude oil, around 50% of its natural gas, and over 90% of its methanol and fertiliser feedstocks. With 401 billion tonnes of coal reserves — among the world's largest — the government sees gasification as a pathway to energy security and import substitution, Information Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said when announcing the scheme, according to Reuters.

Execution Risks Loom Large

The troubled history of the Talcher fertiliser project in Odisha has become a cautionary tale for the sector. The coal-to-fertiliser plant has faced repeated delays and cost overruns, highlighting the execution challenges inherent in India's coal gasification ambitions.

State-run power producer NTPC has signalled interest in entering the coal gasification business, with plans to produce 5–10 million tonnes of synthetic gas per year over the next three to four years, Reuters reported. But scaling from pilot interest to commercial operations remains a significant hurdle.

A pre-application conference held on July 20, 2026, under Additional Secretary Sanoj Kumar Jha, saw enthusiastic participation from public and private sector companies, technology providers, and prospective applicants, the Ministry of Coal said. The deadline for submitting applications is September 7, 2026.

What NRI Investors Should Watch

For diaspora investors tracking India's energy transition, the coal gasification scheme represents both opportunity and caution. The government's projected ₹2.5–3 lakh crore in total investment could open doors for companies in engineering, procurement, and construction. But the industry's demand for guaranteed buyers signals that commercial viability remains unproven — a risk factor worth weighing before committing capital to related sectors.

What's Next

With the application deadline five weeks away, the government faces a choice: address the industry's concerns on offtake guarantees and logistics support, or risk a tepid response to a scheme designed to reshape India's energy landscape. Several countries, including the United States and China, are exploring similar coal gasification technologies, adding competitive pressure to India's timeline.
